## Reflections

::: {.callout-note title="bCourses Submission"}
Submit your answers---to the following reflections---to the corresponding 
assignment in bCourses.

Accepted formats: PDF, HTML, MS Word (`.docx`), or Google Doc
:::


### Reflection 1: Tracking Silent Failures

The Harvard economists skipped 5 entire countries in their key calculation 
because they accidentally misaligned a visual row selection box in Excel.

- Reflect on your own history with spreadsheets or scripts.

- Have you ever committed a silent, unrecorded clerical error that altered 
an assignment or project output?

- Did you catch it through a systematic checking protocol, or was it pure luck?

- What hidden mouse-slip is lurking inside your current active folders right now?


### Reflection 2: Unpacking Status Bias

Reinhart and Rogoff were world-respected Harvard economists. Because of their 
immense prestige, global big-hitters blindly trusted their numbers to pass massive laws.

It took a 28-year-old graduate student checking the actual, raw formula boxes to 
expose that the emperor had no clothes.

- Think about your own data consumption habits.

- Have you ever accepted a chart as "fact" simply because it came from 
a famous journal, a top university, or a respected researcher?

- How will you deliberately adjust your skepticism when reading 
"high-status" science moving forward?


### Reflection 3: Structural Safeguards

Borwein and Bailey demand that journal editors and scientists implement stricter 
standards to stop genuine errors from proliferating.

- Suppose you are the Lead Auditor of your own academic output.

- Draft a personal, non-negotiable **two-rule checklist** that you will enforce 
on your next data project to ensure a spreadsheet or code mismatch is structurally impossible.

- How will you guarantee your future self sticks to these rules when a deadline 
is 3 hours away and stress is at its peak?
